title_page.title: Temporal quantification of atrial fibrillation burden with distribution-free uncertainty intervals: development and multinational external validation
title_page.running_title: Temporal quantification of atrial fibrillation burden
title_page.article_type: Clinical Research Article (digital health / artificial intelligence)

runs.text: Atrial fibrillation (AF) burden is increasingly used to guide care, yet automated tools estimate it by counting time windows classified as AF—a biased estimator of a proportion—and report no uncertainty. We aimed to develop and externally validate a detector-agnostic burden estimator with per-patient uncertainty intervals.

Burden was treated as a per-patient quantity to be estimated. A hidden Markov burden layer (PA-HMMQ) uses the output of any beat-to-beat interval AF detector, models the temporal persistence of rhythm, optionally re-estimates each patient's rhythm dynamics, and provides split-conformal 90% intervals. Three detectors were developed in 243 patients (six US databases) and evaluated, without retraining or recalibration, in 988 patients (8,576 h) from Japan, China and Canada. The analysis plan was pre-registered; the pre-specified primary endpoint was the per-patient absolute burden error in pooled external cohorts.

With the pre-registered emission model, PA-HMMQ did not outperform classify-and-count (3.07 ± 0.30 vs 2.99 ± 0.26 percentage points [pp]). With the emission model selected on development data before the full analysis, the mean error was 2.52 ± 0.24 pp (mean paired difference vs classify-and-count -0.47 pp, 95% CI -0.56 to -0.38), lower than all eight comparators on average and for all three detectors, although rank-based tests were not significant against three of them. The gain came from temporal modelling; per-patient re-estimation of dynamics added nothing. Specificity for AF presence (≥30 s) rose from 0.74 to 0.91 at the cost of sensitivity (0.99 to 0.94). Conformal intervals covered 0.95 of external patients (target 0.90), but only 0.84 in the Japanese cohort. Atrial flutter caused the largest errors.

Modelling rhythm persistence when aggregating detector outputs modestly reduced AF-burden error and false AF diagnoses across three continents and enabled calibrated per-patient intervals; atrial flutter remains the main limitation of RR-based burden estimation.
Atrial fibrillation burden • Ambulatory electrocardiography • Artificial intelligence • Uncertainty quantification • Conformal prediction • External validation

In 988 external patients from Japan, China and Canada, a hidden Markov burden layer placed on top of RR-interval AF detectors reduced the mean absolute AF-burden error from 2.99 to 2.52 percentage points compared with counting AF-classified windows, consistently across three detectors.

The benefit came from modelling the temporal persistence of rhythm; classical prevalence-correction methods and per-patient re-estimation of rhythm dynamics did not help, and recalibrating window probabilities on the development population worsened burden estimates.
False AF diagnoses in AF-free patients fell (specificity 0.74 to 0.91), with a reduction in sensitivity.
Conformal intervals reached nominal 90% coverage of individual patients' burden in two of three external cohorts but under-covered in the third; atrial flutter remained the dominant source of error.

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is increasingly characterised by how much of the time a patient spends in the arrhythmia rather than by its mere presence. AF burden—the proportion of monitored time in AF—is associated with ischaemic stroke and other outcomes, is an endpoint of rhythm-control trials, and has become central to the interpretation of device-detected subclinical AF
. The 2024 European Society of Cardiology guidelines acknowledge burden as a clinically relevant descriptor while noting that its measurement is method-dependent
. With the spread of long-term Holter, patch, wearable and implantable monitoring, burden is now almost always computed automatically.

Automated burden estimation is usually performed by running a window-level AF detector over the recording and counting the windows classified as AF. Beat-to-beat (RR) interval detectors range from classical irregularity statistics
to deep recurrent networks evaluated across geographies
. These studies report excellent window-level discrimination, but burden is a patient-level

, and counting classified windows is a biased estimator of a proportion whenever sensitivity and specificity are imperfect: false-positive windows inflate burden in patients with little AF, false negatives deflate it in patients with persistent AF, and the size of both errors changes with the patient's own AF prevalence
. Recent work has shown that burden derived from averaged detector probabilities degrades under external dataset shift unless probabilities are recalibrated with labelled data from the target cohort

. In addition, current tools report burden as a single number without an uncertainty statement, although a clinician deciding whether a low burden is real needs to know how wrong the estimate could plausibly be.
addresses exactly the problem of estimating class proportions in a new sample whose prevalence differs from that of the training data
, and conformal prediction provides distribution-free uncertainty intervals with finite-sample coverage guarantees
. Neither has, to our knowledge, been applied to AF burden: conformal methods in electrocardiography have so far targeted diagnostic classification
, and quantification estimators assume independent samples, whereas rhythm windows are strongly dependent in time.

We therefore treated AF-burden estimation as a per-patient quantification problem and developed a detector-agnostic burden layer—a hidden Markov model quantifier that models the temporal persistence of rhythm and can re-estimate each patient's rhythm dynamics (patient-adaptive hidden Markov quantifier, PA-HMMQ)—with distribution-free conformal burden intervals. Following a pre-registered plan, we tested in external cohorts from Japan, China and Canada (i) whether it reduces per-patient burden error compared with classify-and-count and established quantification and smoothing methods, (ii) which of its components are responsible, (iii) whether its intervals attain nominal coverage, and (iv) how robust it is to R-peak errors, ectopy and reduced training data.
This was a retrospective development and multinational external-validation study using publicly available, de-identified ambulatory electrocardiogram (ECG) databases. Reporting follows TRIPOD+AI
and the 2025 EHRA/HRS/ESC e-Cardiology scientific statement on artificial intelligence in clinical electrophysiology

; the EHRA AI checklist is provided as Supplementary material. The analysis plan, including hyper-parameters, random seeds, endpoints and statistical tests, was written and version-controlled before any model was trained (Supplementary material S1).
The development pool comprised six PhysioNet databases recorded in the USA
, the MIT-BIH AF Database (AFDB), the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database (MITDB)
, the BIDMC Congestive Heart Failure Database (CHFDB)

, and the MIT-BIH Normal Sinus Rhythm databases (NSRDB, NSR2DB). External validation used three cohorts that were never used for training, calibration or tuning: SHDB-AF, 24-h two-channel Holter recordings of Japanese patients with paroxysmal AF annotated beat-by-beat by a cardiologist
; CPSC2021, dynamic Holter recordings from the 4th China Physiological Signal Challenge
; and Icentia11k, single-lead patch recordings from Canadian outpatients with technologist-reviewed beat and rhythm labels

, from which 800 patients were sampled uniformly at random (fixed seed, without inspecting labels) and their first ten 70-min segments used. Only beat and rhythm annotation files were used (Supplementary Table S1 lists versions, licences and exclusions).
Reference standard and units of analysis

RR intervals were derived from the database beat annotations (automatic R-peak annotations for AFDB and SHDB-AF, reviewed annotations elsewhere); intervals outside 0.2–3.0 s or outside labelled rhythm segments were excluded. Each RR interval inherited the reference rhythm at its terminating beat. RR series were cut into non-overlapping windows of 60 consecutive valid intervals. A window was labelled AF if ≥50% of its duration was annotated AF. The reference AF burden of a patient was the AF-annotated time divided by the analysed time; atrial flutter was counted as non-AF (sensitivity analysis: AF+flutter). Recordings of the same patient were aggregated, so the unit of analysis was the patient.

Because the proposed method operates on any detector's output, three detectors spanning model complexity were trained: (i) Classical-LR, a logistic regression on three classical irregularity features (normalised RMSSD, Shannon entropy, turning-point ratio)

; (ii) LightGBM, gradient-boosted trees on 16 RR features including sample-entropy-based irregularity (pre-specified primary detector); and (iii) RRNet, a convolutional–bidirectional recurrent network on the normalised RR sequence, re-implemented in the spirit of ArNet/ArNet2
(architecture in Supplementary material). Each detector outputs a window probability

the following estimators were compared, all calibrated on held-out development patients only: classify-and-count (CC, threshold 0.5); CC after a three-window median filter (CC-MF); probabilistic CC (PCC, mean probability)
and PCC after source isotonic recalibration (PCC-iso, the label-free analogue of probability recalibration
); adjusted CC (ACC), which corrects CC for the source true- and false-positive rates
; and a two-state hidden Markov model with fixed source rhythm dynamics (HMM-src)

Each patient's window sequence is modelled as a two-state (non-AF/AF) hidden Markov chain. Emission likelihoods are a function of the detector output only and are held fixed (label-shift assumption: the appearance of an AF window does not depend on how much AF the patient has). The rhythm dynamics—initial distribution π
—are re-estimated for every patient by maximum-a-posteriori expectation–maximisation with a Dirichlet prior centred on the source dynamics A
where ξ are the posterior expected transitions and κ (pre-specified 10) the prior strength. Burden is the duration-weighted posterior probability of AF, B̂
). This generalises EMQ (κ→0, no temporal dependence) and HMM-src (κ→∞). The pre-registered version used emission likelihoods estimated as class-conditional histograms of logit(
) on calibration patients; a variant using the detector probability directly as likelihood (e(AF) ∝

) was pre-specified as an ablation. Following a decision rule recorded after a one-seed pipeline check and before the full analysis, and based on development patients only (Supplementary S1, Amendment A1), the variant with the lower development error was designated the final method; both are reported throughout. To isolate the contribution of per-patient adaptation, every PA-HMMQ variant was also compared with the HMM using identical emissions but fixed source dynamics (post hoc). A further post-hoc revision (R1) selected the emission sharpness separately for each detector on calibration patients (likelihood ratio (
Posterior burden samples were drawn by forward-filtering backward-sampling (200 samples)
, giving a model-based standard deviation σ̂
. On a separate set of calibration patients, nonconformity scores r = |B − B̂|/(σ̂ + ε) (ε = 0.002) were computed, and the ⌈(n+1)(1−α)⌉-th smallest score q̂ defined the interval B̂
+ ε), clipped to [0,1], with α = 0.10. Under exchangeability of patients, this guarantees ≥90% marginal coverage
. Constant-width conformal intervals around CC, PCC-iso and PA-HMMQ, and the uncalibrated posterior credible interval, served as comparators.

For each of five pre-specified seeds, development patients were split, stratified by database and AF presence, into training (45%; 15% of these for early stopping), calibration A (15%; all source calibration quantities), calibration B (20%; conformal quantile only) and test (20%) sets. No patient appeared in more than one set. An automated audit fingerprinting all RR windows and recordings across all databases identified one exact duplicate recording in SHDB-AF (two files of the same subject with identical RR series), which was removed (Supplementary Table S1). Features and RR normalisation were computed within each window only.

The pre-specified primary endpoint was the per-patient absolute burden error (percentage points, pp) in the pooled external cohorts with the LightGBM detector. Per-patient errors were averaged over the five seeds and compared between the proposed estimator and each comparator using two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction across the eight comparators
; effect sizes are the mean and median paired differences with patient-level bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (2000 resamples) and matched-pairs rank-biserial correlations
. Secondary endpoints were Bland–Altman bias and limits of agreement

, false burden in AF-free patients, classification of patients by burden thresholds (≥30 s of AF, ≥1%, ≥10%; exact McNemar tests on seed-majority classifications), conformal coverage (Clopper–Pearson 95% CI) and interval width, and window-level discrimination and calibration of the detectors. Summary statistics are mean ± standard deviation over seeds. Analyses not in the pre-registered plan (fair-comparator tests, emission selection R1, exclusion of flutter patients) are labelled post hoc. Robustness was assessed by re-analysing SHDB-AF after simulated missed R peaks (2%, 5%), false R peaks (2%, 5%), R-peak timing jitter (10, 25 ms) and premature beats with compensatory pauses (5%, 10%). Sensitivity analyses varied κ, the training-set size (25%, 50%) and the window length (30, 120 beats). Analyses used Python 3.13 with PyTorch, scikit-learn, LightGBM and SciPy; all code and the commands regenerating every number, table and figure are publicly available (Data availability).

Only publicly available, de-identified databases distributed under open licences were used; the original studies obtained ethical approval and consent as described in the cited publications. No new data were collected, so additional ethical approval and consent were not required.

The development pool comprised 243 patients (4,045 h of analysed RR data; 119 with AF), and the external cohorts 988 patients (8,576 h; 175 with AF and 39 with atrial flutter): SHDB-AF 93 patients (72 with AF during the recording), CPSC2021 105 patients (53 with AF) and Icentia11k 790 patients (50 with AF) (Table 1; Supplementary Figure S1). Ten of the 800 sampled Icentia11k patients had no analysable labelled windows.

All detectors discriminated AF windows well (Supplementary Table S2, Supplementary Figures S2–S4). For LightGBM, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.992 ± 0.005 in the development test set and 0.969 ± 0.003, 0.992 ± 0.001 and 0.990 ± 0.001 in SHDB-AF, CPSC2021 and Icentia11k; window sensitivity and specificity were 0.974 and 0.972 in Icentia11k.

With the pre-registered emission model, PA-HMMQ did not reduce burden error compared with classify-and-count in the pooled external cohorts (3.07 ± 0.30 vs 2.99 ± 0.26 pp; mean paired difference 0.09 pp, 95% CI -0.07 to 0.26; Holm-adjusted P = 0.541) and was worse than median-filtered counting (2.73 ± 0.23 pp) (Table 2; Supplementary Table S14). The primary hypothesis was therefore not supported for the pre-registered specification.

By the development-data rule of Amendment A1, applied before the full analysis, probability emissions were selected (development error 2.858 vs 3.186 pp). This final PA-HMMQ had the lowest mean error of all estimators in each external cohort (Table 2, Figure 2): 4.23 ± 0.11 pp in SHDB-AF, 2.88 ± 0.39 pp in CPSC2021 and 2.27 ± 0.33 pp in Icentia11k, versus 4.51 ± 0.12, 3.85 ± 0.76 and 2.69 ± 0.35 pp for classify-and-count. In the development test set it was not better than the pre-registered variant or the fixed-dynamics HMM (3.04 ± 1.26, 2.97 ± 1.03 and 3.00 ± 1.02 pp).

In the pooled external cohorts, the mean paired difference favoured the final PA-HMMQ over every comparator, with bootstrap 95% CIs excluding zero (Table 4; Supplementary Figure S6): -0.47 pp (-0.56 to -0.38) versus classify-and-count, -0.21 pp (-0.27 to -0.17) versus median-filtered counting and -1.33 pp (-1.50 to -1.16) versus isotonic-recalibrated probability averaging. The pre-specified Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, however, were significant after Holm correction against classify-and-count (P = <0.001), PCC, PCC-iso, EMQ and HMM-src, but not against median-filtered counting (P = 0.229), ACC (P = 0.229) or PACC (P = 0.198). Most external patients were AF-free and received near-zero burden from all estimators, so median paired differences were close to zero; the mean gain was concentrated in patients with AF (3.82 vs 4.49 pp) and in AF-free patients with false-positive windows (mean false burden 2.24 vs 2.66 pp; Table 3).

The ranking was reproduced with the other detectors (Supplementary Tables S3–S4): pooled external error 7.44 ± 0.69 vs 8.54 ± 0.56 pp (Classical-LR) and 3.45 ± 0.70 vs 3.96 ± 0.83 pp (RRNet). Bias was 1.70 pp (classify-and-count 2.00 pp) and Lin's concordance correlation 0.902 (0.900) (Table 3, Figure 3).

Re-estimating rhythm dynamics per patient did not contribute: the final PA-HMMQ and the HMM with the same emissions but fixed source dynamics had identical error (2.52 ± 0.22 pp; mean paired difference 0.00 pp, 95% CI -0.02 to 0.02), and error was insensitive to the prior strength κ (Supplementary Table S5, Supplementary Figure S5). The improvement was therefore attributable to temporal modelling with sharp emission likelihoods. Classical prevalence-correction estimators that ignore temporal dependence (ACC, PACC, EMQ) did not consistently improve on classify-and-count, and recalibrating window probabilities on development patients worsened burden error (PCC-iso 3.85 ± 0.51 pp).

Using the presence of ≥30 s of AF, the final PA-HMMQ increased specificity from 0.744 to 0.914 and decreased sensitivity from 0.992 to 0.941; on seed-majority classifications it corrected 140 patients misclassified by classify-and-count and misclassified 9 that it had classified correctly (exact McNemar P <0.001). For a burden of ≥1%, specificity was 0.923 versus 0.850 and sensitivity 0.971 versus 0.992 (Supplementary Table S7).

Normalised conformal intervals around the final PA-HMMQ covered the reference burden in 0.910 of development test patients and 0.949 (95% CI 0.933–0.961) of external patients (0.843 SHDB-AF, 0.949 CPSC2021, 0.961 Icentia11k); mean width 3.94 pp and median width 1.99 pp (Table 5, Figure 4). Coverage was lower in patients with AF (0.894) than in AF-free patients (0.961). Constant-width conformal intervals around classify-and-count reached similar coverage (0.926) but were much wider (mean 13.97 pp), and uncalibrated posterior credible intervals under-covered (0.834).

Selecting the emission sharpness per detector on calibration patients (Revision R1, post hoc) gave a pooled external error of 2.74 ± nan pp with LightGBM, 11.07 ± nan pp with Classical-LR and [PENDING] pp with RRNet, and did not improve on the A1 specification (Supplementary Tables S5, S15).

In SHDB-AF, errors of all estimators increased with simulated false R peaks and premature beats, while missed beats and timing jitter had smaller effects; the ranking of estimators was largely preserved (Figure 5; Supplementary Tables S9–S10). Reduced training data and 30- or 120-beat windows are reported in Supplementary Table S11.

Errors were largest in patients with intermediate burden and in patients with atrial flutter (Figure 6; Supplementary Tables S6, S13). Of the 988 external patients, 39 had flutter; with an AF+flutter reference the error of the final PA-HMMQ was 1.64 pp, and excluding flutter patients (post hoc) 1.19 pp (classify-and-count 2.11 and 1.67 pp; Supplementary Table S8). Absolute error correlated with flutter burden (Spearman ρ = 0.298) and reference burden (ρ = 0.459), inversely with recording duration (ρ = -0.307), and only weakly with ectopic beats (supraventricular ρ = -0.030; ventricular ρ = 0.108; Supplementary Figure S7). Error did not differ materially by sex or age in SHDB-AF (Supplementary Table S12).

On a 4-core CPU, the burden layer required a median of 244 ms per 24-h recording (288 ms including posterior sampling for the interval), compared with 797 ms for RR-feature extraction and 12 ms for LightGBM inference (Supplementary Figure S8).

In 988 patients from three continents who contributed 8,576 hours of ambulatory recordings, aggregating detector outputs with a hidden Markov burden layer reduced the mean per-patient AF-burden error compared with counting AF-classified windows and with eight alternative estimators, for three detectors of very different complexity, and markedly reduced false AF diagnoses in AF-free patients; conformal calibration produced per-patient intervals whose coverage met the 90% target in two of three external cohorts but fell short in the Japanese cohort. Equally important are the negative findings: the pre-registered specification did not outperform counting, per-patient re-estimation of rhythm dynamics—the component we expected to correct patient-specific prevalence—added nothing, and the absolute improvement was modest.

Burden is a property of a patient's rhythm trajectory: an isolated AF-like window inside long sinus rhythm, or a short regular stretch inside persistent AF, is more likely a classification error than a rhythm change. A temporal model removes much of this window-level noise, which is why median filtering and hidden Markov smoothing improved on counting. The magnitude of the gain depended on how sharply detector outputs were translated into evidence: calibration-set class-conditional histograms flattened the likelihood ratios because window labels near rhythm transitions are noisy, letting sticky source dynamics over-smooth genuine rhythm changes, whereas the detector's own probability preserved discriminating evidence. Contrary to our hypothesis, patient-specific prevalence did not need explicit correction once temporal structure was modelled—with sharp emissions the likelihood dominates the prior over rhythm dynamics, which explains the insensitivity to κ. Quantification estimators designed for independent samples (ACC, PACC, EMQ)

did not reliably improve on counting, and recalibrating window probabilities on the development population made burden estimates worse. A probability calibrated on a development population embeds that population's AF prevalence and pulls every patient's estimate towards it; good classifier calibration is therefore not sufficient for unbiased burden estimation, which complements the observation that recalibration with labelled target data improves probability-based burden
AF burden is increasingly used to stratify risk and to evaluate therapy
, and device- or patch-derived burden informs decisions about subclinical AF

. The clinically most visible effect was the reduction of spurious AF in AF-free patients: with counting, 26% of external patients without ≥30 s of reference AF were assigned ≥30 s of AF (final PA-HMMQ 9%), which in long-term monitoring may trigger further investigation or anticoagulation discussions. This came at the cost of missing some patients with very little AF, a trade-off that should be weighed against the purpose of monitoring. The burden layer requires no retraining of an existing detector, adds well under a second of computation per 24-h recording, and supplies an interval indicating whether a reported burden is distinguishable from zero or from a decision threshold. Because conformal coverage is guaranteed only for patients exchangeable with the calibration set, intervals should be recalibrated locally when a device or population differs substantially, as recently argued for AI-ECG classifiers
Deep RR-interval models such as ArNet and ArNet2
report strong window-level performance and low burden error, and commercial AI burden agrees closely with manual assessment in selected cohorts

. Those studies report point estimates; the present work is complementary, operating on top of any detector, comparing aggregation strategies systematically and adding patient-level uncertainty. Consistent with ArNet2, atrial flutter was the dominant failure mode of RR-based burden estimation

: flutter with variable conduction produces irregular RR intervals indistinguishable from AF without atrial activity information. Whether flutter time should count towards burden is partly definitional—stroke-prevention recommendations for flutter largely follow those for AF
—and with an AF+flutter reference the errors of all estimators fell substantially.

First, the pre-registered specification failed; the final emission model was chosen on development data after a one-seed check (Amendment A1) and the per-detector emission selection (R1) and flutter-exclusion analyses were post hoc, so the external results for the final method, although never used for any decision, should be regarded as requiring confirmation in further cohorts. Second, the improvement was modest (a mean of -0.47 pp versus counting), rank-based tests were not significant against three comparators, and the development test set did not favour the final over the pre-registered variant. Third, the study used retrospective public databases with heterogeneous annotation processes; reference labels, particularly in Icentia11k, may contain errors, and R peaks were taken from database annotations rather than from a uniform detector, although simulated R-peak errors were examined. Fourth, the development pool was modest (243 patients) and from one country. Fifth, conformal coverage is marginal over patients, was lower in patients with AF, and is not guaranteed under distribution shift. Sixth, 60-beat windows limit resolution for episodes shorter than about 30–60 s. Seventh, Icentia11k was represented by a random subset of patients and segments, and the reduced-training and window-length analyses omitted it. Finally, no outcome data were available, and photoplethysmography-based wearables, which are increasingly used for burden monitoring

Accounting for the temporal persistence of rhythm when converting AF-detector outputs into burden modestly but consistently reduced burden error and substantially reduced spurious AF in AF-free patients across Japanese, Chinese and Canadian cohorts and three detectors, and conformal calibration provided per-patient burden intervals with near-nominal coverage in most, but not all, external cohorts. Per-patient re-estimation of rhythm dynamics and classical prevalence-correction methods did not add benefit. Atrial flutter remains the main obstacle to accurate RR-based burden assessment and should be addressed before burden thresholds derived from such tools are applied clinically.

legend.text: Study pipeline. RR intervals derived from ambulatory ECG beat annotations are cut into 60-beat windows and scored by a window-level AF detector. The patient-adaptive hidden Markov quantifier (PA-HMMQ) treats the patient's window sequence as a two-state Markov chain whose rhythm dynamics are re-estimated for each patient (maximum-a-posteriori expectation–maximisation with a prior centred on source dynamics from calibration patients A), and returns the posterior expected burden. Posterior sampling gives a model-based standard deviation that is converted into a 90% conformal interval using calibration patients B. External cohorts are never used for training or calibration.
